A2.text:
Leyla and Elvin love old things. On Sunday, they walked near Gabala. They wanted to see the ruins of an ancient fortress. The weather was warm and sunny.

“Look here,” Elvin said. He pointed to a small hole in the wall. He found a dirty metal coin. It looked very old.

“Wow! Is it from a king?” Leyla asked. “Maybe it is from a different era.”

Elvin cleaned the coin with his shirt. It had strange letters on it. “We are so lucky,” he smiled. “We will make history! Museum people will love this.”

They took the coin to Leyla’s uncle, Rashad. He is a history teacher in Baku. They put the coin on his desk.

Rashad looked at it carefully. Then, he started to laugh very loudly.

“Why are you laughing?” Elvin asked. “Is it fake?”

“No, it is real,” Rashad said. He wiped a tear from his eye. “But it is not from a king. This is a token for a game machine. When I was a teenager in the 1980s, we used these to play video games in the park.”

Leyla and Elvin looked at each other. They did not find a king’s treasure. But they drank tea with Uncle Rashad and listened to his funny stories about his childhood.

B1.text:
Leyla and Elvin always enjoyed exploring historical places in Azerbaijan. Last Sunday, they decided to hike near Gabala to visit the ruins of an ancient mountain fortress. The morning was clear, and the view from the top was incredibly beautiful.

While they were eating their sandwiches, Elvin noticed a small hole in the stone wall. He reached inside and pulled out a heavy metal coin covered in green dirt.

“Look at this artifact!” Elvin said excitedly. He rubbed the coin with his thumb. “Maybe it belongs to a great empire, or it was hidden here during a revolution.”

Leyla examined the strange letters on the metal. “If this is a real treasure, we will go down in history,” she said. “The national museum will definitely want to display it.”

They carefully wrapped the coin in a napkin and took a bus back to Baku. They went straight to see Leyla’s uncle, Rashad, who worked as a historian at the university.

Rashad put on his reading glasses and held the coin under a bright lamp. He turned it over twice, and then a huge smile appeared on his face. He started laughing so hard that he had to sit down in his chair.

“Is it completely worthless?” Elvin asked, feeling a bit disappointed.

“It has no real historical value, but it is a real blast from the past,” Rashad explained, wiping his eyes. “This is not a Roman coin. It is a token for a Soviet arcade machine. Back in the 1980s, I used these to play a game called Sea Battle in the local park.”

Leyla and Elvin did not become famous archaeologists that day. However, Uncle Rashad ordered some pakhlava, poured them tea, and spent the whole evening sharing wonderful stories about his teenage years.

B2.text:
Leyla and Elvin shared a passion for discovering forgotten places. On a crisp Sunday morning, they drove up to Gabala to explore the overgrown ruins of an ancient fortress that overlooked the valley. They spent hours scrambling over mossy stones and discussing the region's turbulent past.

While Elvin was attempting to photograph a crumbling archway, he noticed a deep crevice in the masonry. Reaching inside, his fingers brushed against cold metal. He pulled out a heavy, corroded disk that looked remarkably like a coin.

“Look at this incredible artifact!” Elvin exclaimed, desperately rubbing the grime away with the edge of his jacket. “Judging by the weight, it could be from a lost empire, or maybe it dates back to the era before Russian colonisation.”

Leyla squinted at the faint, worn symbols stamped into the metal. “If we’ve genuinely found a royal coin, we might go down in history,” she grinned. “Imagine our names on a little gold plaque in the National Museum.”

Eager to verify their discovery, they drove straight back to Baku and rushed to the university office of Leyla’s uncle, Rashad, a respected professor of modern history.

Rashad adjusted his spectacles and placed the metal disk under his desk lamp. He examined it in absolute silence for ten seconds. Then, he leaned back in his leather chair and erupted into booming laughter, clapping his hands together.

“Is it a fake, Uncle?” Leyla asked, her shoulders dropping slightly.

“Oh, it’s completely authentic, just not the kind of treasure you were hoping for,” Rashad chuckled, wiping a tear from his eye. “What a blast from the past! I can give you a direct eyewitness account of this item’s use. It isn't a relic of an industrial revolution or an ancient king. It’s a fifteen-kopeck token for a Soviet arcade machine. I used to spend all my pocket money feeding these into the 'Sea Battle' game at the Boulevard in the 1980s.”

Though they hadn't managed to make history, Leyla and Elvin couldn't help but laugh at their own wild imaginations. Uncle Rashad promptly ordered tea and spent the next hour entertaining them with fond memories of his misspent youth.

podcast.title: A trip into the past

before.predict: Do you like history? Guess: where did Leyla go last weekend — a museum, old ruins or a library?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is history. And Leyla has just come back from a trip into the past.
[laugh] Kind of. Last weekend I went to Gabala, to see the ruins of the old city. More than two thousand years ago, it was a capital.
Wow. What can you see there now?
Old walls, stones, the bottom of a tower. It's ancient, so you need some imagination. But the little museum has amazing artifacts — coins, pots, even jewellery.
I love museums like that. Every object tells a story.
What about Manchester? Is there history there?
Lots! Manchester was one of the first cities of the Industrial Revolution. Two hundred years ago, it was full of factories and smoke.
So it changed the world.
It did. That era will always go down in history as the start of the modern world — but life in the factories was very hard, even for children.
At school, did you learn about the British Empire?
Yes, but when I was young, the books only told the proud part. Now we talk more honestly about colonisation and the pain it caused in many countries.
That's important. History isn't only about kings and battles.
Exactly. I think the best history comes from normal people. My grandad gave me an eyewitness account of the day people first walked on the Moon.
Really? What did he say?
He was nineteen. The whole street watched it on one small black-and-white TV. He said people cried. Everyone knew they were watching humans make history.
That's beautiful. Last month my mum found a box of old photos from the eighties. What a blast from the past!
[laugh] Big hair?
Very big hair! And my dad with a moustache. It was like looking at another world.
That's history too. One day our photos will look funny to our grandchildren.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: which moment in history would you like to see with your own eyes — and why?
I'd like to see the Moon landing — on a bigger TV. See you next time!
Bye for now!
